people.name: Ada_Lovelace
people.summary: Ada Lovelace (Augusta Ada King, Countess of Lovelace) was an English mathematician and writer best known for her work on Charles Babbage's proposed Analytical Engine. Educated intensively in mathematics and science by her mother to counteract the perceived 'poetic madness' of her father, Lord Byron, she combined rigorous analysis with an imaginative, philosophical outlook she called 'poetical science'. In 1842–1843 she translated Luigi Menabrea’s article on the Analytical Engine and added extensive Notes that included a detailed algorithm for computing Bernoulli numbers and a far‑reaching vision of machines manipulating symbols to create music, graphics, and more. Although often ill and constrained by Victorian society, she maintained an active network with leading scientists and tried to apply mathematics even to gambling, before dying at 36 from uterine cancer.

people.name: Alan_Turing
people.summary: Alan Turing was an English mathematician and codebreaker whose work founded modern computability theory, helped break German wartime ciphers at Bletchley Park, and shaped early computer design and artificial intelligence research. His later career also produced influential ideas in mathematical biology. He was prosecuted for homosexual acts in 1952 and died in 1954 from cyanide poisoning.

people.name: Albert_Einstein
people.summary: Albert Einstein (1879–1955) was a German-born theoretical physicist whose work transformed modern understandings of space, time, matter, and energy. While working at the Swiss Patent Office he published his 1905 “Annus Mirabilis” papers, including special relativity and the mass–energy relation E=mc², and a key explanation of the photoelectric effect. He later developed the general theory of relativity, received the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics, emigrated from Nazi Germany to the United States, and used his worldwide fame to advocate for peace, international cooperation, and nuclear arms control.

people.name: Antoni_Gaudí
people.summary: Antoni Gaudí i Cornet was a Catalan architect and designer, the leading figure of Catalan Modernisme. Working largely in Barcelona, he developed a highly personal style rooted in natural forms, craft traditions, and an increasingly intense Catholic spirituality. He is best known for transforming the Sagrada Família into his lifelong project.

people.name: Cunigunde_of_Luxembourg
people.summary: Cunigunde of Luxembourg (c. 975 – 3 March 1040) was a noblewoman of the House of Ardenne–Luxembourg who became queen of Germany and later Holy Roman Empress as the wife of Henry II. Celebrated for her piety and political acumen, she was a close adviser to Henry, appeared frequently in royal charters as consors regni (“partner in rule”), and played a notable role in imperial church patronage, especially at Bamberg. After acting briefly as regent following Henry’s death in 1024, she retired to the Benedictine monastery she had founded at Kaufungen, where she lived a life of prayer and charity until her death.

people.name: E._T._A._Hoffmann
people.summary: E. T. A. Hoffmann (Ernst Theodor Amadeus Hoffmann) was a German Romantic writer whose fantastical and gothic tales reshaped European fiction, while he simultaneously pursued a career as a Prussian jurist. He was also active as a composer, conductor, music critic, and visual artist, moving between administrative posts and theater work amid the upheavals of the Napoleonic era. His Berlin years produced many of his best-known works, including stories later adapted for major operas and ballets.

people.name: Edsger_W._Dijkstra
people.summary: Edsger W. Dijkstra was a Dutch computer scientist whose ideas reshaped programming methodology, algorithms, and operating systems. He helped establish disciplined approaches to program design and correctness, and his research influenced both academic computer science and practical system building. He received the 1972 ACM Turing Award for foundational contributions to structured programming and programming languages.

people.name: Emmy_Noether
people.summary: Emmy Noether (1882–1935) was a German mathematician whose work transformed abstract algebra and profoundly influenced mathematical physics. At Erlangen and later at Göttingen she developed the modern theory of rings, ideals, and modules, introduced the notion of Noetherian structures, and proved Noether’s theorems linking symmetries with conservation laws in physics. Barred for years from paid academic posts because she was a woman and Jewish, she nonetheless led a renowned school of algebraists before being dismissed by the Nazis and continuing her research and teaching at Bryn Mawr College and the Institute for Advanced Study in the United States.

people.name: Erich_Kästner
people.summary: Erich Kästner was a German writer, poet, and screenwriter whose witty, socially observant work ranged from Weimar-era satire to enduring children’s classics such as "Emil and the Detectives" and "Das doppelte Lottchen". He remained in Germany under National Socialism despite bans on his books, continuing to work under pseudonyms, and re-emerged after 1945 as a leading public intellectual and editor in Munich. In later decades he received major international recognition, including the Hans Christian Andersen Award.

people.name: Frances_Allen
people.summary: Frances E. Allen was an American computer scientist whose foundational work on optimizing compilers and automatic parallelization reshaped modern software and high-performance computing. Over a 45-year career at IBM she led major compiler and parallel computing projects, becoming the first woman IBM Fellow and the first woman to receive the ACM A. M. Turing Award. She was also a committed mentor and advocate for women and other underrepresented groups in computing.

people.summary: Frank Lloyd Wright was an American architect whose long career reshaped modern architecture through the Prairie School, Usonian housing ideas, and major works such as Fallingwater and the Guggenheim Museum design. He also wrote widely and trained generations of apprentices through the Taliesin Fellowship.

people.name: Franz_Kafka
people.summary: Franz Kafka (1883–1924) was a German-language Jewish writer from Prague whose unsettling, precise prose reshaped 20th‑century literature. Trained as a lawyer and employed in insurance, he wrote fiction in his spare hours, portraying isolated protagonists trapped in opaque bureaucratic systems. Only a handful of works, including "The Metamorphosis" and the story collections "Contemplation" and "A Country Doctor", appeared during his lifetime, but they influenced generations of writers, philosophers, and artists. His early death from tuberculosis left his novels unfinished and his reputation to grow posthumously from near-obscurity to global prominence.

people.name: Frei_Otto
people.summary: Frei Otto was a German architect, structural innovator and professor whose experimental work with cable nets, gridshells and other tensile structures transformed 20th‑century architecture. Starting from gliding and prisoner‑of‑war camp construction, he developed a lifelong quest for building with minimal material, energy and environmental impact, founding the Institute for Lightweight Structures in Stuttgart and shaping icons such as the Munich Olympic roofs and the German pavilion at Expo 67. A leading voice of organic and ecological design, he received the Pritzker Architecture Prize in 2015, shortly before his death.

people.name: Friedensreich_Hundertwasser
people.summary: Friedensreich Hundertwasser (born Friedrich Stowasser) was an Austrian artist best known for vividly colored paintings, graphic works, and idiosyncratic architectural designs that rejected straight lines and standardization. Marked by wartime survival and decades of travel, he developed an artistic worldview centered on organic form and the rights of nature. From the 1970s onward he became a prominent environmental voice and designed influential buildings that integrated vegetation and irregular, human-centered forms.

people.name: Georg_Wilhelm_Friedrich_Hegel
people.summary: Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel was a German philosopher and the culminating figure of German idealism, known for an ambitious system spanning logic, nature, spirit, history, art, religion, and politics. His university career developed from early theological studies and private tutoring through professorships at Jena, Heidelberg, and Berlin, where his lectures and major books established him as a central thinker of modern philosophy.

people.name: Grace_Hopper
people.summary: Grace Hopper was an American computer scientist, mathematician, and U.S. Navy rear admiral who became one of the earliest programmers of the Harvard Mark I, a creator of the first working compiler, and a key figure in the development of FLOW-MATIC and COBOL, foundational high-level programming languages. Over a parallel academic, industrial, and naval career spanning more than four decades, she championed machine-independent, English‑like programming and helped standardize programming language practices across the U.S. Navy and the computing industry.

people.name: Hedy_Lamarr
people.summary: Hedy Lamarr (born Hedwig Eva Maria Kiesler) was an Austrian-born American film star whose MGM career peaked from the late 1930s through the 1950s. During World War II she co-invented, with composer George Antheil, a frequency-hopping “secret communication system” intended to prevent jamming of radio-guided torpedoes—an early spread-spectrum concept. In later decades she withdrew from public life but received belated recognition for her inventive work while still alive.

people.name: Heinz_Nixdorf
people.summary: Heinz Nixdorf (1925–1986) was a German computer pioneer and entrepreneur who founded Nixdorf Computer AG and built it from a tiny start‑up into a major international electronics and computing company. Coming from a poor railway family and interrupted by wartime service, he fought his way back to complete secondary school, study applied physics, and gain crucial experience in calculator development at Remington Rand. With early backing from the utility RWE, he created Germany’s first tube‑based computer, then shifted to transistor and semiconductor technology, becoming a leading figure of the German Wirtschaftswunder and a key promoter of decentralized data processing and workforce training until his sudden death at a trade fair in 1986.

people.name: Henry_II
people.summary: Henry II of the Ottonian dynasty rose from Duke of Bavaria to King of Germany and Italy and then Holy Roman Emperor. Ruling with his wife Cunigunde, he pursued a strongly church-centered kingship, founded the diocese of Bamberg, and fought prolonged wars on the empire’s eastern frontier, especially against the Polish ruler Bolesław I. He died childless after a reign marked by close cooperation with leading bishops and popes and significant ecclesiastical reforms.

people.name: John_von_Neumann
people.summary: John von Neumann was a Hungarian‑American mathematician, physicist, computer scientist, and engineer whose work reshaped pure mathematics, quantum mechanics, game theory, economics, and the architecture of modern digital computers. A child prodigy from Budapest, he became one of the youngest Privatdozenten in Germany, then a founding professor at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton. During World War II and the early Cold War he was central to the Manhattan Project, the development of high‑speed computing, and U.S. nuclear and missile strategy. He died in 1957 from metastatic cancer.

people.name: Joseph_Weizenbaum
people.tagline: Creator of ELIZA, Critic of AI
people.summary: Joseph Weizenbaum was a German‑American computer scientist and a prominent critic of unreflective faith in computers and artificial intelligence. After emigrating from Nazi Germany to the United States in 1936, he studied mathematics, worked as a system engineer at General Electric, and joined MIT in 1963, where he helped develop early list‑processing languages and contributed to the ARPANET. His 1960s program ELIZA became a landmark in natural‑language processing and led him to question the social and ethical implications of AI, themes he explored in his influential 1976 book "Computer Power and Human Reason." In later life he became a leading public intellectual on technology and responsibility, eventually returning to live in Berlin in 1996, where he remained active until his death in 2008.

He later founded one of Germany’s earliest computer firms and pursued ideas in computing theory alongside artistic work.

His company, founded during the Gold Rush era, grew from a merchant operation into a major manufacturer of durable workwear.

people.name: Marie_Curie
people.summary: Marie Curie was a Polish-born physicist and chemist who built her career in France and transformed the study of radioactivity. She discovered the elements polonium and radium with Pierre Curie, introduced key concepts and measurement methods for radioactive phenomena, and won Nobel Prizes in both Physics and Chemistry. During World War I she advanced battlefield radiology, and later led major research institutions while promoting international scientific cooperation.

people.name: Steve_Jobs
people.summary: Steve Jobs was an American entrepreneur, inventor, and investor who co-founded Apple and helped pioneer the personal-computer revolution. After being forced out of Apple in 1985, he founded NeXT and became the controlling owner of Pixar, guiding it to success with computer-animated films. He returned to Apple in 1997 and led a dramatic corporate revival, overseeing landmark products including the iPod and iPhone before stepping down due to illness.

people.name: Umberto_Eco
people.summary: Umberto Eco was an Italian medievalist, philosopher and semiotician who became internationally famous as the author of the novel The Name of the Rose and as a leading theorist of semiotics, mass media, and contemporary culture. Trained in medieval philosophy, he developed influential ideas about the “open work,” interpretative semiotics, and fascism, while teaching at major Italian universities and writing widely read fiction and essays.

people.name: Zaha_Hadid
people.summary: Zaha Hadid (1950–2016) was an Iraqi‑British architect, artist, and designer whose radical, fluid forms reshaped late‑20th‑ and early‑21st‑century architecture. Educated in mathematics in Beirut and in architecture at the Architectural Association in London, she first became known for visionary, largely unbuilt projects and for her role in the deconstructivist movement. With works such as the Vitra Fire Station, the MAXXI Museum in Rome, the Guangzhou Opera House, and London’s Aquatics Centre, she translated her dynamic paintings into complex built structures worldwide. The first woman to win the Pritzker Architecture Prize and the RIBA Royal Gold Medal, she combined avant‑garde experimentation with large‑scale public and cultural commissions.
